newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - D.Babcock falls on restructuring news.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - D.Babcock falls on restructuring news.

text.p: Shares in troubled German engineering firm Deutsche Babcock AG fell almost 17 percent at one point on Monday after it said restructuring costs would be higher than originally expected.

Babcock shares have lost almost two-thirds of their value in the last year and slipped to a low on Monday of 45 marks. In late electronic trade they showed a loss of 14 percent on the day, down 7.50 at 46.50.

"We're gradually getting used to hearing worse and worse news from Babcock," said one share trader. Axel Luther, analyst at BHF Bank, added: "Every three months the company releases a new and worse outlook."
Babcock approved a restructuring plan in July to spin off non-core businesses after it said it was expecting a loss of 400 million marks ($260 million) for the 1995/96 financial year to September 30.
Analysts said news that restructuring would cost more than had been estimated could push those losses above 400 million marks.

"The restructuring is happening too slowly and the company structure is still not clear and should be changed," said one analyst, who asked not to be named. "The management haven't got things in control."
The restructuring, expected to include the sale of 20 of Babcock's 60 subsidiaries, is being aided by a 600 million mark German bank credit line.
"The restructuring is going to be very difficult and the process will take at least another three years," said Richard Schramm, analyst at Trinkaus and Burkhardt in Dusseldorf.
"The banks have taken Babcock under their wing to try to save what is saveable."
Two weeks ago, Babcock said it had made 180 million marks through the disposal of its 50 percent stake in the Canadian group Velan Inc, Bergesmann GmbH and Bergesmann USA Inc.
It said 110 million of that would be booked by the end of the current fiscal year.
But on Monday Babcock said the closure of its Magdeburg plant and personnel changes in its piping unit and its U.S. operations would all cost more than original estimates.
"One minute we get good news and the next bad. They should have told us about this earlier," said Luther.
Analysts said the company needed to sell several subsidiaries as soon as possible -- for example, its 70 percent stake in speciality machinery maker Schumag, which is very profitable.
"Babcock has a few large good parts and lots of small bad parts," said Luther.
In a management report to the company's supervisory board, Babcock said subsidiaries operating in its core business would meet profit targets this year.
The German engineering sector has suffered from high wages and an overvalued mark. Most analysts expect it to pick up next year but Schramm said that would not be enough for Babcock.
"At its core Babcock has some good businesses but it must get rid of its loss-making parts soon," added Luther. ($1=1.5309 Mark)
